cards.q: Where is your progress saved?
cards.a: In this browser, on this machine. It is not an account, and it does not leave the page.
cards.why: In this browser, on this machine. It is not an account, and it does not leave the page. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “How to use this campus”?
cards.a: One file, a track order, and a way to know what you have finished.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What is the course trying to produce?
cards.a: Someone who can frame a task, choose a model and tools, evaluate the result, and hand the evidence to another person.
cards.why: Someone who can frame a task, choose a model and tools, evaluate the result, and hand the evidence to another person. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “What you are learning to do”?
cards.a: The skill is judgment you can show, not a tour of product names.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Which field is the file another person can open later?
cards.a: The artifact. The trace explains how you got there. The metric says how it scored.
cards.why: The artifact. The trace explains how you got there. The metric says how it scored. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Keep proof for every exercise”?
cards.a: Run, trace, metric, and artifact: four fields that make a lesson repeatable.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: When is a tool allowed to send email on its own?
cards.a: It is not. Sending waits for a person, even if the draft looks correct.
cards.why: It is not. Sending waits for a person, even if the draft looks correct. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Safety rules for every exercise”?
cards.a: Private data stays local until you have a reason to move it, and some actions always wait for a person.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Is an API key required to study?
cards.a: No. Add a local model or a hosted API only when an exercise needs a live call.
cards.why: No. Add a local model or a hosted API only when an exercise needs a live call. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “What you need on your machine”?
cards.a: A current browser is enough to study. A local model is optional and comes later.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why does fine-tuning come after evals?
cards.a: Because you need a measured failure of prompting and retrieval before training is a rational cost.
cards.why: Because you need a measured failure of prompting and retrieval before training is a rational cost. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “How the tracks fit together”?
cards.a: Models, then prompting, then a way to ground and act, then proof that it worked.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why can a fluent answer still be false?
cards.a: Because the model is continuing likely text. Likelihood is not a citation.
cards.why: Because the model is continuing likely text. Likelihood is not a citation. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “A model predicts the next token”?
cards.a: Fluency is the product of a probability model. It is not a source of record.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why is 'about 0.75 words per token' not a budget?
cards.a: It is an English-prose average, not a count for your model, your language, or your code.
cards.why: It is an English-prose average, not a count for your model, your language, or your code. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Tokens are the unit of cost and context”?
cards.a: A token is a chunk of text, not a word, and every limit you hit is counted in tokens.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Who shares the context window?
cards.a: The instructions, the retrieved or pasted sources, the conversation, and the tokens the model still has to write.
cards.why: The instructions, the retrieved or pasted sources, the conversation, and the tokens the model still has to write. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “The context window is one shared budget”?
cards.a: Instructions, retrieved text, the conversation, and the answer all spend the same token limit.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Does a low temperature stop hallucinations?
cards.a: No. It reduces random variation. A likely-but-wrong token can still be the top choice.
cards.why: No. It reduces random variation. A likely-but-wrong token can still be the top choice. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Temperature is a sampling control”?
cards.a: Lower settings repeat likely tokens. Higher settings take more risks. Neither setting checks facts.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What do you score instead of the model's confidence?
cards.a: Whether the answer matches a source, a tool result, or a known test case.
cards.why: Whether the answer matches a source, a tool result, or a known test case. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Hallucination is fluent text without evidence”?
cards.a: Catch it with sources, tools, and tests. Do not catch it by asking the model if it is sure.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Where do tool results belong?
cards.a: In a tool message, separate from the user's request, so the model can see what the tool returned.
cards.why: In a tool message, separate from the user's request, so the model can see what the tool returned. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “System, user, and tool messages do different jobs”?
cards.a: Put standing rules in the system message. Put the task in the user message. Put tool results in tool messages.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why do you pin a model id?
cards.a: Because a family name hides version changes that move quality, cost, and safety.
cards.why: Because a family name hides version changes that move quality, cost, and safety. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Model families you will see in 2026 job posts”?
cards.a: Hire and design for a role, then pin an id. A family name is not a version.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What should you try before you switch on a slower reasoning model?
cards.a: A fast model on a fixed set of examples, after the prompt and output shape are clear.
cards.why: A fast model on a fixed set of examples, after the prompt and output shape are clear. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Choose a reasoning model or a fast chat model”?
cards.a: Spend extra compute when the task needs a plan. Do not spend it on extraction you can score cheaply.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What makes a done-check real?
cards.a: A person or a test can apply it to the output without asking the model whether it tried hard.
cards.why: A person or a test can apply it to the output without asking the model whether it tried hard. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Write the job, the input, and the done-check”?
cards.a: A prompt is a job description. If you cannot tell whether the answer succeeded, the prompt is not finished.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why validate in code if you asked for JSON?
cards.a: Because the model can still wrap it in prose, drop a bracket, or invent a key. The schema mode reduces that. It does not replace the check.
cards.why: Because the model can still wrap it in prose, drop a bracket, or invent a key. The schema mode reduces that. It does not replace the check. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Lock the output shape”?
cards.a: Ask for a structure, then validate it in code. Prose that looks like JSON is not JSON.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why include a refusal example?
cards.a: Because otherwise every example shows a successful extraction, and the model learns to fill gaps.
cards.why: Because otherwise every example shows a successful extraction, and the model learns to fill gaps. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Few-shot examples that do not leak”?
cards.a: Examples teach the pattern. They are also data you might not have permission to send.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: When is a fixed workflow the better design?
cards.a: When you can name the steps in advance and test each one. Choice belongs in a loop only when the next action depends on what came back.
cards.why: When you can name the steps in advance and test each one. Choice belongs in a loop only when the next action depends on what came back. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Split a hard task into steps you can test”?
cards.a: One prompt that plans, searches, calculates, and drafts is several jobs hiding in a paragraph.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What is the revision allowed to change?
cards.a: Only the lines that failed the checklist.
cards.why: Only the lines that failed the checklist. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Critique the draft, then revise once”?
cards.a: A second pass helps when the critique is a checklist, not a request to 'make it better'.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why is the model not the security boundary?
cards.a: Because it is trained to follow instructions it reads. Code has to restrict tools, validate arguments, and gate side effects.
cards.why: Because it is trained to follow instructions it reads. Code has to restrict tools, validate arguments, and gate side effects. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Prompt injection is untrusted text that pretends to be an order”?
cards.a: Documents, web pages, and tool descriptions can carry instructions. Your system does not have to obey them.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why run the old passing cases after a prompt edit?
cards.a: Because the edit can fix the example you stared at and damage the rest.
cards.why: Because the edit can fix the example you stared at and damage the rest. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Change one thing, then score it”?
cards.a: A prompt edit without a before-and-after score is a new opinion.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Does local mean more accurate?
cards.a: No. It means you control where the weights run and where the prompt goes. Accuracy is an eval result.
cards.why: No. It means you control where the weights run and where the prompt goes. Accuracy is an eval result. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Run a model locally when the data should stay put”?
cards.a: Local is a privacy and latency choice. It is not automatically the more accurate choice.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Where should a personal lab listen?
cards.a: On localhost. A model service bound to every network interface is a different, riskier setup.
cards.why: On localhost. A model service bound to every network interface is a different, riskier setup. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Install a runner and call it on localhost”?
cards.a: Ollama and llama.cpp are the usual local runners. The smoke check is a local HTTP call or a CLI completion.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why not start with the largest model you can find?
cards.a: Because a model that does not fit does not run, and a model that barely fits leaves no room for context.
cards.why: Because a model that does not fit does not run, and a model that barely fits leaves no room for context. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Pick a model size that fits in memory”?
cards.a: If the weights do not fit, the runner will swap, crash, or refuse. Start smaller than your pride.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What does Q4 tell you by itself?
cards.a: That the weights were stored at about 4 bits. Not whether the model passes your tasks.
cards.why: That the weights were stored at about 4 bits. Not whether the model passes your tasks. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Quantization trades precision for fit”?
cards.a: The weights are stored with fewer bits. You measure whether your tasks still pass.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Does downloadable mean you may sell a product that hides the model inside?
cards.a: No. That depends on the license that came with those weights.
cards.why: No. That depends on the license that came with those weights. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Read the license before you ship a weight”?
cards.a: Open weights are not one license. Some allow commercial use. Some restrict it. Some restrict use of the outputs for training.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What should you check before you rewrite a prompt that 'suddenly failed'?
cards.a: That the runner is up and the model id matches the one in your last good artifact.
cards.why: That the runner is up and the model id matches the one in your last good artifact. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Keep a smoke test you can rerun”?
cards.a: After a reboot, prove the runner is up before you debug the prompt.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Which of the three belongs in git?
cards.a: Prompts and fixtures that contain no secrets and no private corpus. Not weights. Not private notes.
cards.why: Prompts and fixtures that contain no secrets and no private corpus. Not weights. Not private notes. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Keep weights, prompts, and private data apart”?
cards.a: Different files, different backups, different permissions.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What do you do if a key lands in a log?
cards.a: Revoke it, then fix the log. Keeping the key and editing one file is not enough if the log was copied.
cards.why: Revoke it, then fix the log. Keeping the key and editing one file is not enough if the log was copied. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Call an API without putting the key in the repo”?
cards.a: The key lives in an environment or a secret store. The client reads it at runtime. Logs do not print it.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What can a schema guarantee?
cards.a: Shape. Not truth, and not that an id exists in your corpus.
cards.why: Shape. Not truth, and not that an id exists in your corpus. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Ask for structured output and check it”?
cards.a: Schema mode is a feature of the API. Your parser is still the gate.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why is an immediate retry of a 429 a mistake?
cards.a: The provider asked you to slow down. Immediate retries spend the same quota faster and can make the block longer.
cards.why: The provider asked you to slow down. Immediate retries spend the same quota faster and can make the block longer. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Set timeouts, retries, and a rate-limit plan”?
cards.a: A hung call is a product bug. A retry storm is a bill.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why is cost per call the wrong product number?
cards.a: Because failed calls, retries, and human cleanup are part of the real cost of a successful task.
cards.why: Because failed calls, retries, and human cleanup are part of the real cost of a successful task. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Read the bill in tokens, cache, and batch”?
cards.a: Cost is a property of the design. Input tokens, output tokens, and tool calls are the levers.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What must stay constant when you swap providers?
cards.a: The tasks, the checks, and the fields you record. Otherwise you are comparing prompts, not providers.
cards.why: The tasks, the checks, and the fields you record. Otherwise you are comparing prompts, not providers. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Compare providers on the same ten tasks”?
cards.a: Swap the client. Keep the fixture, the schema, and the scorecard.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Name two fields that belong in a model-call log and one that does not.
cards.a: Belong: model id and token counts, or latency and status. Does not: the API key, or a private document you have no approval to store.
cards.why: Belong: model id and token counts, or latency and status. Does not: the API key, or a private document you have no approval to store. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Log the call without logging the secret”?
cards.a: Keep the model id, the latency, the token counts, and a hash or id of the prompt. Drop the key and the raw private text unless you have a place to store it.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: When should the system refuse?
cards.a: When the retrieved passages do not contain the answer, even if the model could guess.
cards.why: When the retrieved passages do not contain the answer, even if the model could guess. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Retrieve when the answer has to come from a source”?
cards.a: Retrieval-augmented generation finds passages first, then asks the model to answer from those passages.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why is there no universal best chunk size?
cards.a: Because the right boundary is the structure of the document and the questions you ask, which you measure.
cards.why: Because the right boundary is the structure of the document and the questions you ask, which you measure. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Chunk documents so a citation can point at them”?
cards.a: Split on structure. Keep a stable id. Do not hunt for a magic token count.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What do you re-embed when you change embedding models?
cards.a: The whole corpus. Old vectors are not comparable to new ones.
cards.why: The whole corpus. Old vectors are not comparable to new ones. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Search with keywords and with embeddings”?
cards.a: Embeddings find similar meaning. Keywords find the exact name. Hybrid search uses both.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What failure can a reranker not repair?
cards.a: A first stage that never retrieved the right chunk.
cards.why: A first stage that never retrieved the right chunk. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Rerank a short list before you prompt”?
cards.a: Retrieve widely, then keep the few passages that actually answer.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What makes a citation checkable?
cards.a: It names an id you retrieved and a place in that source a person can find.
cards.why: It names an id you retrieved and a place in that source a person can find. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Cite a passage a person can open”?
cards.a: A citation is an id and a span, not a confident tone.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: A fluent answer cites nothing and sounds right. Where do you look first?
cards.a: At whether any retrieved chunk contained the claim. If none did, the failure is retrieval or refusal, not prose style.
cards.why: At whether any retrieved chunk contained the claim. If none did, the failure is retrieval or refusal, not prose style. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Failure modes to test before you tune the prompt”?
cards.a: Wrong chunk, stale chunk, lost middle, and a corpus that never contained the fact.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why score retrieval separately from the answer?
cards.a: Because a wrong passage cannot be saved by the writer, and a right passage can still be ignored. The two failures have different fixes.
cards.why: Because a wrong passage cannot be saved by the writer, and a right passage can still be ignored. The two failures have different fixes. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Measure retrieval before you measure the answer”?
cards.a: Recall on the right chunk is a different number from whether the paragraph was helpful.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What turns a model call into an agent?
cards.a: A loop that can call tools, observe results, and stop on a rule you set.
cards.why: A loop that can call tools, observe results, and stop on a rule you set. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “An agent is a loop with a stop rule”?
cards.a: The model may call a tool, read the result, and repeat, until an answer or a cap.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Who enforces the schema, the model or your code?
cards.a: Your code. The model only proposes the call.
cards.why: Your code. The model only proposes the call. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Give every tool a name, a schema, and a handler”?
cards.a: The model proposes a call. Your code checks the arguments and runs the handler.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why an allowlist instead of a denylist?
cards.a: New tools stay unavailable until you classify them. A denylist treats silence as permission.
cards.why: New tools stay unavailable until you classify them. A denylist treats silence as permission. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Allow, deny, and ask a person”?
cards.a: Read-only tools can run inside the cap. Anything that leaves the machine waits.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Is a vector store the same as the chat thread?
cards.a: No. The thread dies with the task. A store remains, and it needs a retention rule.
cards.why: No. The thread dies with the task. A store remains, and it needs a retention rule. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Decide what the agent is allowed to remember”?
cards.a: The thread, a file, and a store are different lifetimes. Pick one on purpose.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What has to cross the boundary between two agents?
cards.a: A structured artifact, not an open-ended chat, plus a narrower tool list on each side.
cards.why: A structured artifact, not an open-ended chat, plus a narrower tool list on each side. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Add another agent only when the handoff is a real artifact”?
cards.a: Two agents that share a vague chat are one confused loop with extra cost.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: The summary says a file was not touched. The trace shows a write call. Which do you believe?
cards.a: The trace. Then you find out why the summary hid it.
cards.why: The trace. Then you find out why the summary hid it. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Read the trace, not the closing summary”?
cards.a: Every tool call, argument, result, and approval is a line you can reconstruct.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why is a calculator easier to retry than a send-email tool?
cards.a: A second calculation returns the same number. A second send delivers a second email.
cards.why: A second calculation returns the same number. A second send delivers a second email. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Make tool calls safe to retry, inside a sandbox”?
cards.a: A second run of the same call should not double-send, double-charge, or escape the folder.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Is the MCP server the language model?
cards.a: No. The server exposes capabilities. The model runs in the host and asks the client to call the server.
cards.why: No. The server exposes capabilities. The model runs in the host and asks the client to call the server. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “MCP connects a model to tools you did not hard-code”?
cards.a: The Model Context Protocol is a standard way for an app to talk to a tool server.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Where should a database password live?
cards.a: On the server, in its environment. Not in the prompt, and not in a tool description.
cards.why: On the server, in its environment. Not in the prompt, and not in a tool description. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Host, client, and server have different jobs”?
cards.a: The person uses the host. The client holds the session. The server does the work.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why is a resource still a safety issue if it cannot write?
cards.a: Because its text enters the model's context and can carry instructions. Read-only is not the same as trusted.
cards.why: Because its text enters the model's context and can carry instructions. Read-only is not the same as trusted. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Tools act, resources are read, prompts are templates”?
cards.a: Use the primitive that matches the risk.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What does stdio mean for where the server runs?
cards.a: On the same machine, as a child process of the host, with the power of the environment you gave it.
cards.why: On the same machine, as a child process of the host, with the power of the environment you gave it. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Connect a local server over stdio”?
cards.a: The host starts a process and speaks MCP on its standard streams. The process is the trust boundary.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why is a tool description a safety boundary?
cards.a: Because it is inserted into the model's context. A hostile description is an instruction the model may follow.
cards.why: Because it is inserted into the model's context. A hostile description is an instruction the model may follow. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “Consent, authentication, and untrusted servers”?
cards.a: A server you did not review can read what the host will hand it, and its tool text can steer the model.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Does connecting an issue tracker via MCP remove the need to review the diff?
cards.a: No. It adds context. The change to the repo is still reviewed against tests and intent.
cards.why: No. It adds context. The change to the repo is still reviewed against tests and intent. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “How coding tools use MCP”?
cards.a: Editors and agents use MCP to reach issue trackers, browsers, docs, and internal APIs. The repo is still reviewed by a person.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: What is the result of a coding agent, the summary or the diff?
cards.a: The diff, plus the test command you ran. The summary is a claim about them.
cards.why: The diff, plus the test command you ran. The summary is a claim about them. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.

cards.q: Which sentence is the point of “A coding agent edits a repository under rules”?
cards.a: It can read, propose a plan, change files, and run commands. Your rules say which of those happen alone.
cards.why: That sentence is this lesson's summary. The others belong to different lessons.

cards.q: Why name a test in the goal?
cards.a: Because that command is the done-check. A green test is evidence. A summary is not.
cards.why: Because that command is the done-check. A green test is evidence. A summary is not. That is the check this lesson asks you to keep.
